title: NRI Property in India: 8 FEMA Rules Every Diaspora Buyer and Seller Must Know
excerpt: From permitted property types to repatriation caps and Power of Attorney pitfalls, a comprehensive guide to the Foreign Exchange Management Act rules governing NRI real estate transactions in India.
body:
• NRIs can freely buy residential and commercial property in India without RBI permission, but agricultural land, plantations, and farmhouses are strictly prohibited under FEMA
  • All payments must route through NRE, NRO, or FCNR accounts — cash payments can attract penalties of up to three times the transaction value
  • Repatriation of sale proceeds is capped at $1 million per financial year from NRO accounts, with a lifetime limit of two residential properties

Non-Resident Indians looking to buy or sell property in India face a web of regulations under the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999 — and getting the details wrong can be expensive. With penalties reaching up to three times the transaction value for procedural non-compliance, understanding these rules is not optional for any diaspora member considering Indian real estate.

Here are the eight essential FEMA rules every NRI buyer and seller should know.

1. What You Can and Cannot Buy

Under FEMA, NRIs and Overseas Citizens of India (OCIs) can freely purchase residential and commercial properties in India. There is no cap on the number of properties or their combined value. However, the restriction on agricultural land, plantation property, and farmhouses is absolute. There are no exceptions based on intent, location, or corporate structure — an NRI cannot circumvent the prohibition by buying through an Indian company in which they hold shares.

Agricultural land received through inheritance can only be sold to a person resident in India who is an Indian citizen.

2. Payment Channels Are Non-Negotiable

All payments for property acquisition must go through permitted banking channels under FEMA. Acceptable sources include inward remittances via SWIFT transfer and funds held in NRE, NRO, or FCNR(B) accounts. Foreign currency cash payments, traveller's cheques, and any mode not specifically permitted under FEMA are illegal.

For most NRIs, NRE accounts offer the cleaner funding route since they hold foreign earnings converted to rupees and are fully repatriable. NRO accounts hold Indian-sourced income such as rent and dividends.

3. The $1 Million Repatriation Cap

When an NRI sells property in India, the sale proceeds must be credited to an NRO account first. Repatriation from NRO accounts is capped at $1 million per financial year. For properties purchased using NRE account funds, the repatriation amount cannot exceed the foreign currency equivalent of the original purchase price.

Crucially, repatriation benefits for residential properties are limited to a maximum of two properties in a lifetime. The remitter must submit a prescribed undertaking and a certificate from a Chartered Accountant in the format specified by the Central Board of Direct Taxes.

4. Tax Implications Have Changed

Capital gains tax rules shifted materially with India's Budget 2024. For properties purchased on or after July 23, 2024, long-term capital gains (on property held over 24 months) are taxed at 12.5% without indexation benefit. Properties purchased before that date allow buyers to choose between 12.5% without indexation or 20% with indexation, whichever results in lower tax.

TDS on NRI property sales is deducted at 20% (plus surcharge and cess) on long-term capital gains and 30% on short-term gains — significantly higher than the 1% rate for resident sellers under Section 194-IA.

5. Power of Attorney Requires Careful Handling

Most NRIs complete property transactions without visiting India in person, relying on a Power of Attorney (PoA) to authorize a representative. The PoA document must be notarised in the country of residence and attested by the Indian Embassy or Consulate before it is valid in India.

"Assign PoA only to someone whose instructions you can verify independently; misuse of PoA is one of the more common sources of NRI property fraud."

— Brigade Group, NRI Property Investment Guide

6. RERA Verification Is Essential

Before making any payment on an under-construction property, NRIs should verify the project's RERA (Real Estate Regulatory Authority) registration through the respective state portal. A registered project must display its RERA number on all marketing materials. Buying before RERA registration removes all statutory protections.

Checking the developer's delivery history on previous projects through the state RERA portal provides a more reliable indicator than sales brochures.

7. Home Loans Are Available But Structured Differently

Most scheduled banks and housing finance companies offer dedicated NRI home loan products. Key parameters include loan-to-value ratios of 75-90%, tenures up to 20 years, and mandatory repayment through NRE or NRO accounts using inward remittance. SBI, HDFC, ICICI, and Axis Bank all have dedicated NRI teams facilitating remote transactions.

8. Encumbrance Certificate Is Your Safety Net

The Encumbrance Certificate (EC) is the most underrated document in NRI property transactions. It shows the property's full transaction history and any outstanding loans or legal claims registered against it. Combined with an independent title search covering at least 30 years, it forms the baseline due diligence that separates a safe investment from a potential legal quagmire.

The Bottom Line for NRI Buyers

India's real estate market continues to attract NRI investment, with cities like Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, and Chennai showing consistent rental demand and capital appreciation — Hyderabad's Kokapet corridor recorded roughly 12% annual growth in Q1 2026. But the regulatory framework demands precision. FEMA compliance, proper payment channels, and independent legal due diligence are the baseline that protects the investment from the most common failure modes.

NRIs should verify current tax rates with a chartered accountant familiar with both Indian tax law and the applicable Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement before committing to any purchase or sale.
